status: Seed set for editorial review. Meanings cite the defining authority when one exists; 'No legal definition' when none does. Not reviewed for publication.
generalQuestions: What can you tell me about the {protein}? Where does it come from?
Is there a case label or invoice you could show me? Most kitchens are happy to.

beef: Where does the beef come from?
pork: Where does the pork come from?
poultry: Where does the chicken (or duck) come from?
finfish: Is the fish wild or farmed, and from which country?
shellfish: Is it wild or farmed, and from which country?
other: Where does it come from, and is it wild or farmed?

addOnAsk: If I add the {addon}, where is it from?

questions: Is the shrimp wild or farmed?
Which country is it from?
askMerges.merged: Is the shrimp wild or farmed, and which country is it from?

questions: Where is it farmed?
Who certified it organic?
askMerges.merged: Where is it farmed, and who certified it organic?

entries.meaning: A place where the animal was raised or the seafood was caught or farmed. Country-of-origin labeling rules define origin for meat and seafood sold in stores (USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service).
entries.authority: USDA country-of-origin labeling rule — stores only, not restaurants
entries.gap: Restaurants don’t have to follow country-of-origin labeling rules, so a place name on a menu can describe a style or a past supplier rather than what is in the kitchen today.
questions: Is it coming from there right now, or does that change with the season?
Who do you buy it from?

entries.meaning: Caught in the Gulf of Mexico (also called the Gulf of America) by U.S. or Mexican boats. ‘Gulf’ names a body of water, not a country.
entries.gap: ‘Gulf shrimp’ is sometimes used for a style of shrimp, and much of the shrimp served in the U.S. is imported. The word alone doesn’t say which country’s boats caught it.
questions: Is this shrimp domestic or imported?
Is it wild-caught Gulf shrimp, or farmed?

stateNote.AL: Alabama requires restaurants to tell diners when shrimp is imported (National Fisherman, 2025). If the menu doesn’t say, it’s fair to ask.
stateNote.LA: Louisiana requires restaurants to tell diners when shrimp or crawfish is imported (National Fisherman, 2025). If the menu doesn’t say, it’s fair to ask.
stateNote.MS: Mississippi requires restaurants to disclose imported seafood (National Fisherman, 2025). If the menu doesn’t say, it’s fair to ask.
stateNote.TX: Texas requires restaurants to disclose imported seafood (National Fisherman, 2025). If the menu doesn’t say, it’s fair to ask.

entries.meaning: A statement about country. On a retail label, ‘Product of USA’ now means born, raised, slaughtered and processed in the U.S. (USDA rule, effective 2026).
entries.authority: USDA — applies to labels, not menu copy
entries.gap: On a menu nobody checks the wording, and ‘domestic’ may mean processed here rather than raised here.
questions: Which country was it raised or caught in?
Does the case it came in say ‘Product of USA’?

entries.meaning: Raised or caught nearby. There is no legal definition; one federal loan program uses ‘under 400 miles or the same state’ (2008 Farm Bill).
entries.gap: ‘Local’ can mean one feature dish or the whole menu, and the distance is up to the kitchen.
questions: What does local mean here — how far away?
Which dishes use the local meat or fish?

entries.meaning: A named farm, ranch, fishery or supplier — someone the kitchen can tell you more about.
entries.gap: A named supplier may cover one cut or one dish, not everything on the plate or menu. Supplier names are brands, not certifications.
questions: Is everything in this dish from them, or just the feature item?
How long have you bought from them?

entries.meaning: The menu names a farm, ranch, brand or place. FAT can’t verify where this name sources from.
entries.gap: A name alone doesn’t say where the farm is, or whether it’s the farm itself or a distributor’s brand.
questions: Where is {name} located?
Is it the farm itself, or a distributor’s brand?

entries.meaning: The animal ate grass. On a retail label USDA requires documentation for the claim; the old USDA grass-fed standard was withdrawn in 2016.
entries.authority: USDA animal-raising claims guideline (2024) — labels only
entries.gap: Grass-fed doesn’t say whether the animal was finished on grain, or how much of its life was on pasture.
questions: Grass-fed and grass-finished, or finished on grain?
Where was it raised?

entries.meaning: The animal ate grass and forage through to slaughter, with no grain finishing. On labels USDA asks for documentation; third parties (AGA, PCO) certify it.
entries.authority: USDA animal-raising claims guideline (2024) — labels only
entries.gap: On a menu nobody checks the claim, and it doesn’t say where the animal was raised. Much grass-finished beef sold in the U.S. is imported.
questions: Is it certified grass-fed by anyone, or is that the supplier’s description?
Which country was it raised in?

entries.meaning: Raised with time on pasture. USDA approves the claim on labels from the producer’s own documentation; certifiers like Certified Humane set outdoor-space minimums.
entries.authority: USDA animal-raising claims guideline (2024) — labels only
entries.gap: There’s no federal minimum for days or space on pasture, and the claim says nothing about feed.
questions: Is the supplier certified for pasture-raised, or is that their own description?
How much of the year are the animals outside?

entries.meaning: For poultry, USDA requires that birds had access to the outdoors. ‘Cage-free’ means not raised in cages; meat chickens in the U.S. are not caged anyway.
entries.gap: Free range sets no minimum for outdoor time or space, and ‘access’ can be a door the birds rarely use.
questions: Who raises the chicken?
Is the farm certified by anyone for how the birds are kept?

entries.meaning: The animal received no antibiotics. On labels USDA requires documentation for the claim (2024 guideline).
entries.authority: USDA animal-raising claims guideline (2024) — labels only
entries.gap: It doesn’t say anything else about how the animal was raised. Sick animals that need treatment are usually moved to a different program.
questions: Is that verified by a third party, or the supplier’s claim?
Who’s the supplier?

entries.meaning: No growth hormones were used. Federal rules already ban hormones in pork and poultry, so USDA requires those labels to say so. For beef the claim needs documentation.
entries.gap: For chicken and pork the claim is true of all of it. For beef it doesn’t say anything about feed, antibiotics, or how the animal was raised.
questions: Is the beef from a certified program, or the supplier’s description?
Where was it raised?

entries.meaning: On a retail label, USDA ‘natural’ means minimally processed with no artificial ingredients. It is about processing, not how the animal lived.
entries.gap: ‘Natural’ says nothing about feed, antibiotics, outdoor access or where the animal came from.
questions: What does natural mean for this dish — how was the animal raised?
Who’s the supplier?

entries.meaning: A welfare statement. On labels USDA requires documentation, usually a third-party standard. On a menu there is no definition.
entries.gap: It doesn’t say whose standard is used or what it requires.
questions: Is the supplier certified by anyone — Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved, or GAP?
What does humane mean for this farm?

entries.meaning: The birds were cooled with cold air after slaughter instead of in chilled water baths.
entries.gap: It describes processing only — not how or where the birds were raised.
questions: Who raises the chicken?
Where is the farm?

entries.meaning: The liver of a duck or goose that, in conventional production, was fattened by force-feeding (gavage). California and New York City have passed sales bans.
entries.gap: The menu won’t say which farm produced it or how the birds were fed.
questions: Which farm is the foie gras from?
Is it from a farm that doesn’t force-feed?

entries.meaning: Meat from young calves, usually male dairy calves. Housing ranges from group pens to individual stalls.
entries.gap: ‘Veal’ alone doesn’t say how the calves were housed or fed.
questions: Were the calves raised in group housing?
Who’s the supplier?

entries.meaning: Caught in the wild rather than farmed. U.S. country-of-origin labeling rules require stores to say whether seafood is wild or farmed (7 CFR Part 60).
entries.authority: USDA country-of-origin labeling rule — stores only, not restaurants
entries.gap: Restaurants don’t have to follow country-of-origin labeling rules. Wild doesn’t say where it was caught, how, or whether that fishery is well managed.
questions: Where was it caught, and how — line, net, or trap?
Is it wild today, or does that change with the season?

entries.meaning: Raised on a fish or shellfish farm. U.S. country-of-origin labeling rules require stores to say whether seafood is wild or farmed.
entries.authority: USDA country-of-origin labeling rule — stores only, not restaurants
entries.gap: Farmed doesn’t say which country, what kind of farm (net pens, ponds, tanks), or whether it’s certified.
questions: Which country is the farm in?
Is the farm certified — ASC or BAP?

entries.meaning: Names how the seafood was caught. Hook-and-line, trap and hand-diving are generally lower-bycatch methods; ‘day boat’ means the boat returns the same day.
entries.gap: The method is the supplier’s description — a menu doesn’t say who caught it or where. ‘Diver scallops’ is sometimes used for large scallops that were dredged.
questions: Do you know the boat or fishery it came from?
Where was it caught?

entries.meaning: A Japanese method of killing fish quickly with a spike to the brain, often followed by draining the blood. It’s used for quality and is generally faster than suffocation on ice.
entries.gap: It doesn’t say where or how the fish was caught.
questions: Where was the fish caught, and by whom?
Was it done on the boat or after landing?

entries.meaning: On a retail label, FDA ‘fresh’ means never frozen or heat-preserved (21 CFR 101.95).
entries.gap: Fresh doesn’t say how many days since catch, or where from. Fish frozen at sea can be higher quality than ‘fresh’ fish shipped for days.
questions: Was it frozen at any point?
When did it come in?

entries.meaning: The restaurant considers the source sustainable. There is no legal definition; certifiers (MSC, ASC, BAP) and ratings (Seafood Watch) each use their own standards.
entries.gap: It doesn’t say whose standard, or what was checked.
questions: Sustainable by whose standard — MSC, Seafood Watch, or your own?
Where was it caught or farmed?

entries.meaning: The fishery is certified by the Marine Stewardship Council, and the supply chain holds MSC chain of custody.
entries.gap: Only a restaurant with MSC chain of custody can use the label; otherwise it describes the supplier’s product as bought.
questions: Is the restaurant MSC chain-of-custody certified, or is it the supplier?
Which fishery is it from?

entries.meaning: The farm is certified by the Aquaculture Stewardship Council (ASC) or Best Aquaculture Practices (BAP).
entries.gap: Certification covers the farm and supply as bought. BAP uses star levels — one star covers only the processing plant.
questions: Which farm is it, and in which country?
If it’s BAP, how many stars?

entries.meaning: A rating from Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch (Best Choice, Good Alternative, Avoid) or Ocean Wise. These rate a species-and-method combination, not a supplier.
entries.authority: Monterey Bay Aquarium / Ocean Wise (ratings, not certification)
entries.gap: The rating applies to a specific source and method; it’s only accurate if the kitchen’s supply matches it.
questions: Which source is it — where and how was it caught?
Does it change when you switch suppliers?

entries.meaning: For meat and poultry, USDA Organic requires organic feed, no antibiotics or hormones, and outdoor access (7 CFR Part 205).
entries.gap: The dish and the restaurant are not certified — only the ingredient as bought.
questions: Is it USDA Organic certified? Which supplier?
Is the whole dish organic, or just this ingredient?

variants.meaning: USDA has no organic standard for seafood, and FDA doesn’t run organic labeling, so ‘organic’ on fish can’t mean USDA Organic. Organic salmon is farmed: the claim usually means a European or UK organic certification covering the farm’s feed and practices. It can’t carry the USDA Organic seal.
variants.gap: The menu doesn’t say where the fish was farmed or who certified it.
questions: Where is it farmed?
Who certified it organic?
Is the feed organic, or the whole farm?

entries.meaning: A third-party welfare certification (Certified Humane, A Greener World’s Animal Welfare Approved, Global Animal Partnership, American Humane, ROC). Each sets its own standard.
entries.gap: Standards differ a lot — some require outdoor access, some don’t. Certification covers the supplier’s product, not the restaurant.
questions: Which certification, and which level?
Who’s the supplier?

entries.meaning: A brand program of the American Angus Association. Cattle must be mostly black-hided and meet marbling and size specifications.
entries.authority: American Angus Association (brand program, USDA-verified specs)
entries.gap: It’s about breed appearance and eating quality — not where or how the cattle were raised.
questions: Where was the beef raised?
Do you know the packer or ranch?

entries.meaning: A breed name. In the U.S. ‘Angus’ usually means mostly black-hided cattle, not a DNA test.
entries.authority: USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service (Angus claims for live cattle)
entries.gap: Breed says nothing about where or how the animal was raised, or its grade.
questions: What grade is it — Prime or Choice?
Where was it raised?

entries.meaning: USDA quality grades (Prime, Choice, Select) measure marbling and maturity. Prime is the top grade.
entries.gap: Grade is about eating quality only — not breed, feed, origin, or how the animal was raised. ‘Prime rib’ is a cut and need not be Prime grade.
questions: Is it USDA-graded Prime, or is ‘prime’ the name of the cut?
Where was it raised?

entries.meaning: Japanese cattle breeds. Japanese Wagyu is graded A1–A5 by the Japan Meat Grading Association. ‘American Wagyu’ is usually a Wagyu-Angus cross.
entries.authority: No U.S. legal definition (American Wagyu Association sets its own registry rules)
entries.gap: Wagyu can be a crossbreed raised anywhere; the share of Wagyu genetics isn’t stated.
questions: Is the Wagyu Japanese, American, or Australian?
Is it full-blood or a cross — what percent?

entries.meaning: A Japanese regional designation: Tajima-strain cattle born, raised and processed in Hyōgo Prefecture, certified by the Kobe Beef Marketing and Distribution Promotion Association.
entries.authority: Kobe Beef Marketing and Distribution Promotion Association (Japan)
entries.gap: Very little genuine Kobe beef is exported to the U.S. ‘Kobe-style’ is not Kobe beef.
questions: Is it certified Kobe beef? Do you have the certificate number?
If it’s Kobe-style, where was it raised?

entries.meaning: A traditional breed. ‘Heritage’ has no federal definition; The Livestock Conservancy defines heritage chicken and turkey. Kurobuta is the Japanese name for Berkshire pork.
entries.authority: No legal definition (breed associations certify some breeds)
entries.gap: A breed name doesn’t say how the animal was raised, fed, or housed.
questions: Who raises it, and is the breed certified by the breed association?
Are the animals raised outdoors?

entries.meaning: Spanish Iberian pork. Spanish law (Real Decreto 4/2014) uses colored labels: black (100% Iberian, acorn-fed), red (cross, acorn-fed), green (pasture with feed), white (farm-raised).
entries.gap: ‘Ibérico’ alone can be the white-label, farm-raised category. ‘Bellota’ means acorn-finished.
questions: Which label color is it — black, red, green, or white?
Is it 100% Ibérico or a cross?

entries.meaning: Salmon on U.S. menus is usually Atlantic salmon, which is almost all farmed; the U.S. Atlantic salmon fishery is closed. Wild salmon is usually Pacific (king, sockeye, coho).
entries.gap: ‘Salmon’ alone doesn’t say the species, whether it’s wild or farmed, or which country the farm is in.
questions: Is the salmon wild or farmed today?
Which species of salmon is it, and from which country?

entries.meaning: Pacific salmon species. Sockeye and coho on U.S. menus are usually wild; king (chinook) can be wild from Alaska or the Pacific Northwest, or farmed (for example in New Zealand).
entries.gap: The species name doesn’t say wild or farmed, or where it was caught.
questions: Is it wild or farmed?
Where was it caught?

entries.meaning: Species names on the FDA Seafood List. Only Lutjanus campechanus may be called ‘red snapper.’
entries.gap: Snapper and grouper are among the fish most often substituted in restaurants (Oceana, 2013 and 2019). ‘Pacific red snapper’ is usually rockfish.
questions: What species is the snapper, exactly?
Where was it caught?

entries.meaning: The FDA allows ‘white tuna’ only for albacore. In sushi restaurants ‘white tuna’ is often escolar, a different fish that can cause stomach upset.
entries.gap: The menu name may not match the species served (Oceana, 2013).
questions: Is the white tuna albacore or escolar?
Where was it caught?

entries.meaning: Tuna species differ a lot: Atlantic bluefin is managed under catch quotas (ICCAT) and is also ‘ranched’ — caught wild and fattened in pens. ‘Ahi’ is yellowfin or bigeye.
entries.authority: FDA Seafood List; NOAA / ICCAT quotas
entries.gap: ‘Tuna’ or ‘toro’ doesn’t say which species, ocean, or whether it was ranched.
questions: Which species is the tuna, and which ocean?
Is it wild-caught or ranched?

entries.meaning: Patagonian or Antarctic toothfish. ‘Chilean sea bass’ is an FDA-accepted market name; the fish isn’t a bass. Imports require NOAA catch documentation (CCAMLR).
entries.gap: The name doesn’t say which fishery. Some toothfish fisheries are MSC certified; others aren’t.
questions: Which fishery is it from — is it MSC certified?
Is it Patagonian or Antarctic toothfish?

entries.meaning: ‘Sea bass’ covers several species. Branzino (European sea bass) and barramundi on U.S. menus are mostly farmed; black sea bass and striped bass are often wild.
entries.gap: ‘Sea bass’ doesn’t name the species, and doesn’t say wild or farmed.
questions: Which species of bass is it?
Is it wild or farmed, and where from?

entries.meaning: Real crab is a named species (blue, Dungeness, king, snow, Jonah). ‘Kani,’ ‘krab’ and surimi are made from processed pollock or other fish.
entries.authority: FDA — imitation crab must be labeled as imitation at retail
entries.gap: Lump crab meat is often imported pasteurized blue swimming crab, not Chesapeake blue crab.
questions: Is it real crab or imitation? Which species?
Where is the crab meat from?

entries.meaning: Most shrimp served in the U.S. is imported and farmed. Wild U.S. shrimp comes mostly from the Gulf and South Atlantic.
entries.gap: ‘Shrimp’ alone doesn’t say wild or farmed, or which country.
questions: Is the shrimp wild or farmed?
Which country is it from?

stateNote.AL: Alabama requires restaurants to tell diners when shrimp is imported (National Fisherman, 2025). If the menu doesn’t say, it’s fair to ask.
stateNote.LA: Louisiana requires restaurants to tell diners when shrimp or crawfish is imported (National Fisherman, 2025). If the menu doesn’t say, it’s fair to ask.
stateNote.MS: Mississippi requires restaurants to disclose imported seafood (National Fisherman, 2025). If the menu doesn’t say, it’s fair to ask.
stateNote.TX: Texas requires restaurants to disclose imported seafood (National Fisherman, 2025). If the menu doesn’t say, it’s fair to ask.

entries.meaning: Sea scallops in the U.S. are mostly wild Atlantic scallops; Japanese (Hokkaido) scallops are often ranched. ‘Dry-packed’ means no phosphate soak. U10 is a size (under 10 per pound).
entries.gap: Size and packing don’t say where they were harvested or how.
questions: Where are the scallops from?
Are they dry-packed?

entries.meaning: In the U.S., ‘caviar’ alone means sturgeon roe; other roe must name the fish (FDA). International trade in sturgeon caviar is controlled under CITES, and most caviar sold today is farmed.
entries.gap: Menus rarely say the species, the farm, or the country. Kaluga is usually a farmed hybrid from China.
questions: Which species and which farm is the caviar from?
Is it farmed, and in which country?

entries.meaning: Beluga sturgeon is critically endangered. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has barred imports of beluga caviar from the Caspian and Black Sea since 2005.
entries.authority: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; CITES
entries.gap: On a menu ‘beluga’ may mean a farmed beluga, a hybrid, or a brand name. The menu won’t say.
questions: What does beluga mean here — which species, and is it farmed?
Which farm or producer is it from?

entries.meaning: Whatever fish the kitchen bought that day.
entries.gap: The menu names no species, place, or method.
questions: What’s the fish today, and where is it from?
Is it wild or farmed?

knownSources.note: Listed by U.S. distributor The Educated Fish Co. as EU-certified Scottish organic salmon (distributor’s claim, not verified by FAT).
